stem:
A 6-year-old with asthma on medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid has had no daytime symptoms, no night waking, no activity limitation, and reliever use of one day per week over the past 4 months.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the inhaled corticosteroid abruptly today
options.explanation: Abrupt cessation risks loss of control. A preventer is stopped only after about 6 months symptom-free, and this child still uses a reliever weekly.

options.label: B
options.text: Step down to the lowest dose that keeps control
options.explanation: Three or more months of good control means the preventer can be stepped down to the lowest dose that controls symptoms, with a review 4–6 weeks later.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to oral montelukast as the sole preventer
options.explanation: Swapping a working preventer for a less effective one when control is good risks relapse.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a long-acting beta-agonist to consolidate the gains
options.explanation: A LABA is added when control is poor on inhaled corticosteroid alone, not when control is already good.

options.label: E
options.text: Continue the current dose indefinitely without review
options.explanation: Leaving a child on a fixed dose indefinitely misses the chance to minimise steroid exposure.

context:
About 3 months of good control means step down to the lowest dose that holds it, then review in 4-6 weeks. Stop the preventer only after about 6 months symptom-free.

Check technique and adherence before calling the dose a failure. Most poor control is missed doses or a poor device.
